- **RW2 & RQ2 Baseline comparability**

The reviewer raises an important point about consistency in the experimental setup. We agree that this can be explained more clearly and will update the manuscript accordingly. For clarity, we provide the exact details below:

1.  For the probing experiment, we adopt both the reported numbers and the exact setup from [1]. To ensure fidelity, we also run the authors’ provided code and confirm that no hyperparameters are inadvertently missed. Additionally, we train a backbone of similar size to the baseline models to maintain comparability.
2.  For the full fine-tuning setup, we follow the results and comparable configuration from [2]. The reviewer correctly notes that some baselines use only a single conformer during pre-training, which may affect fairness. To address this, we pre-trained a new backbone using a single conformer and repeated the evaluation (Table 2). We report the comparison between the 1-conformer backbone, the original 3-conformer backbone, and the next two best-performing baselines on average. For the remaining baselines, we refer to Table 2 in the manuscript.


**Table 2: 1 Conformer vs. 3 Conformer Setup**

| Method       | BBBP     | Tox21    | ToxCast  | SIDER    | Clintox  | MUV      | HIV      | BACE     | Average  |
| ------------ | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- |
| MoleculeSDE  | 71.8     | 76.8     | 65.0     | 60.8     | 87.0     | 80.9     | 78.8     | 79.5     | 75.1     |
| MoleBlend    | 73.0     | 77.8     | 66.1     | 64.9     | 87.6     | 77.2     | 79.0     | 83.7     | 76.2     |
| Ours (3Conf) | 78.9     | 84.2     | **71.7** | **62.5** | **83.7** | **82.5** | 77.9     | 78.6     | **77.5** |
| Ours (1Conf) | **88.6** | **84.7** | 71.3     | 61.8     | 73.1     | 75.9     | **78.9** | **78.8** | 76.6     |

Although there is a slight decrease in performance under this setup, our method continues to achieve the highest results relative to the other baselines, further demonstrating the robustness and consistency of our approach.

Interestingly, the 1-conformer setup performs slightly better on BBBP, Tox21, and ToxCast, which may indicate that additional conformers introduce noise, as these are generated using RDKit.

We must also note that these models are pre-trained on the PCQM4Mv2 dataset from the OGB Large-Scale Challenge (3.37M molecules), while our backbone was trained on the considerably smaller dataset GEOM, placing our approach at a disadvantage.

---

**RW3 & RQ3 Choice of encoders not well justified**

We agree that SchNet is not the most recent or powerful 3D encoder available, and we clarify our choice in the following. Our initial use of SchNet was motivated by two considerations:

1. To ensure a fair comparison in the full fine-tuning setup (Table 2), we adopted the same encoders (GIN and SchNet) as used by prior baselines.
2. Since our architecture stacks a transformer on top of the encoder, we only require scalar features for the 3D embeddings. Using a more complex encoder, such as EGNN or GemNet, would introduce additional vectorial features and computational overhead without a clear benefit in our current setup.

Nonetheless, following the reviewer’s suggestion, we have pre-trained a new backbone using PaiNN [3] instead of SchNet. PaiNN was chosen because it provides both scalar and vectorial features separately, allowing us to use the scalar features directly with minimal adaptation. It is also among the most recent models in this category.

**Table 3: Evaluation of C-FREE pre-trained using PaiNN vs. SchNet encoder**
| Method        | BBBP     | Tox21    | ToxCast  | SIDER    | Clintox  | MUV      | HIV      | BACE     | Average  |
| ------------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- |
| MoleculeSDE  | 71.8     | 76.8     | 65.0     | 60.8     | 87.0     | 80.9     | 78.8     | 79.5     | 75.1     |
| MoleBlend    | 73.0     | 77.8     | 66.1     | **64.9**     | **87.6**     | 77.2     | 79.0     | 83.7     | 76.2     |
| Ours (+SchNet)         | 78.9     | 84.2     | **71.7** | 62.5     | 83.7     | **82.5** | 77.9     | 78.6     | 77.5     |
| Ours (+PaiNN) | **88.9** | **86.2** | **71.6** | **64.8**     | **87.6**     | 75.7     | **81.4** | 82.3     | **79.8** |

Using PaiNN leads to a substantial performance improvement, demonstrating that our framework can readily benefit from more powerful 3D encoders.

---

* **RW4 Missing Recent Baseline Comparisons.**

We incorporated the results for these recent baselines in the revised manuscript, and the relevant comparisons are provided below.

- For ChemBERTa and MolFM, we report results on the MoleculeNet dataset using its original setup (see Table 4).
- For UniMol2, we report results on the QM9 dataset under the same evaluation protocol.
- We are also running an evaluation on PCQM4Mv2 to enable a comparison with GEM-2. Due to the time constraints of the rebuttal period, these results are still in progress; however, we will include them in the final version of the paper.

**Table 4: Full Fine-tuning on MoleculeNet**

| Method        | BBBP     | Tox21    | ToxCast  | SIDER    | Clintox  | MUV      | HIV      | BACE     | Average  |
| ------------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- |
| ChemBERTa-1   | 64.3     | 72.8     | -        | -        | 73.3     | -        | 62.2     | -        | -        |
| ChemBERTa-2   | 72.8     | -        | -        | -        | 56.3     | -        | -        | 79.9     |          |
| MolFM         | 72.9     | 77.2     | 64.4     | 64.2     | 79.7     | 76.0     | 78.8     | 83.9     | 74.6     |
| UniMol (1)    | 72.9     | 79.6     | 69.6     | 65.9     | 91.9     | 82.1     | 80.8     | **85.7** | 78.5     |
| SCAGE         | 73.4     | 79.4     | 69.3     | 66.0     | **92.7** | -        | -        | 85.4     | -        |
| VideoMol      | 70.7     | 78.8     | 66.7     | **66.3** | -        | -        | 79.4     | 82.4     | -        |
| Ours          | 78.9     | 84.2     | **71.7** | 62.5     | 83.7     | **82.5** | 77.9     | 78.6     | 77.5     |
| Ours (+PaiNN) | **88.9** | **86.2** | **71.6** | 64.8     | 87.6     | 75.7     | **81.4** | 82.3     | **79.8** |

On 4 of the 8 MoleculeNet datasets, our initial pre-trained backbone achieves the strongest performance. Following Reviewer cps9’s suggestion, we also evaluate a variant that replaces the SchNet 3D GNN with the more recent PaiNN model. This version further improves our results and achieves the best overall average performance across the benchmark.

We also note that these baselines were pre-trained on substantially larger and different datasets (UniMol on 19M molecules from multiple sources; MolFM and ChemBERTa on PubChem with 77M molecules), while our method uses a much smaller pre-training set (GEOM with 330K molecules). Even with this difference in scale, our model achieves stronger performance on most targets, which highlights the effectiveness of our design.

We have added these results, along with their standard deviations, to the current revision of the paper in Table 2, Section 4.2.1.

---

* **RW5 Theoretical Results as Support for General Graph Settings.**

The reviewer’s observation about the limited practical impact of WL-based expressiveness on molecular tasks is accurate. In molecular settings, increases in WL expressive power often lead to only modest performance improvements, a trend also reflected in recent work (e.g., Pellizzoni et al., 2025 [5]), which reports that molecular property prediction usually does not benefit from higher-order WL expressiveness. 

We include the theoretical component because it highlights two aspects of the framework. In the 2D-only setting, adding ESAN-Deepsets leads to measurable improvements, which shows that this component can help in tasks where 2D topology has a stronger influence. At the same time, even though these expressiveness gains matter less for molecules, the overall design is not specific to chemistry, and the theory helps show how it can extend to other types of graph problems. We discuss this further in Section 4.3, Ablation on Predictor Types.

---

* **RW6 Overstating and misusing “Contrast-free”, missing information in the diagrams.**

The reviewer is correct that predictor-target asymmetry introduces an implicit form of alignment that is related to self-distillation. Our use of the term “contrast-free” follows the standard terminology in the representation learning literature, where methods such as BYOL, DINO, and JEPA are described as contrast-free because they avoid explicit contrastive objectives [6,7], large negative sets, and the large batch requirements of InfoNCE-style losses. We use the term in the same sense here: our model does not rely on negative pairs, large batch sizes, or explicit contrastive objectives, which helps avoid the computational overhead and instability often seen in contrastive training. We will clarify this terminology in the supplementary material of the final version to avoid any ambiguity. We have added a discussion regarding "contrast-free" methods in Appendix A7.

We thank the reviewer for pointing out the missing elements in the figure. We have updated Figure 1 to highlight the construction of the multimodal sequence and added a new Figure 5, which illustrates the two fine-tuning strategies.

summary.value: This paper introduces C-FREE (Contrast-Free Representation learning on Ego-nets), a self-supervised molecular graph pretraining framework that integrates both 2D topology and 3D conformational information without using contrastive or generative objectives. The key idea is to predict the embeddings of subgraphs (ego-nets) from their complementary neighborhoods, trained in a latent predictive space using a hybrid GINE + SchNet + Transformer architecture. The approach avoids negative sampling, clustering (e.g., METIS), and expensive data augmentations. Empirical evaluations on MoleculeNet, Kraken, and Drugs-75K show strong performance in both classification and regression, often surpassing contrastive and generative baselines. The method also demonstrates label efficiency in low-data regimes and supports multimodal transfer between 2D and 3D settings.

strengths.value:
- The model achieves competitive or superior performance across several benchmarks (MoleculeNet, Kraken, Drugs-75K), including both frozen and fine-tuned evaluations. Notably, even the 2D-only variant performs strongly, indicating robust representation learning.
Comprehensive evaluation
- The experiments are extensive: frozen vs. full fine-tuning, multimodal vs. unimodal ablations, low-label settings, and theoretical expressiveness studies. This provides a well-rounded validation of the approach.
- The paper is well-organized, and implementation details, dataset choices, and ablations are clearly presented. Promises to release code and checkpoints further strengthen reproducibility.

weaknesses.value:
- While the paper emphasizes “contrast-free multimodal learning,” the overall framework is a relatively straightforward adaptation of existing JEPA/BYOL principles with molecular-specific encoders. The main novelty lies in applying ego-nets rather than METIS clusters and fusing 2D/3D modalities, a valuable but not significant step.
- The paper does not sufficiently dissect how 3D information improves over 2D or why multimodal fusion works. Results indicate 3D contributes more, but mechanistic or representational analyses (e.g., embedding alignment, modality redundancy) are absent.
- Some benchmarks (e.g., MoleculeNet [1]) are relatively small and saturated.
- More recent large-scale baselines (like ChemBERTa-2 [2] , Uni-Mol 2 [3], GEM-2 [4], MolFM [5]) are not compared.
- Theoretical results (expressiveness > 1-WL) are interesting but neither novel nor essential to the main empirical contributions. They don’t directly translate into new design insights or explain performance improvements.
- While generally clear, some methodological sections are dense and formula-light. Diagrams (e.g., Fig. 1–2) could better illustrate modality fusion and prediction flow. “Contrast-free” might be slightly overstated, as the predictor/target asymmetry still performs implicit alignment akin to self-distillation.

summary.value: This paper proposes a simple SSL framework, C-FREE, which integrates 2D topology and 3D structural information for learning high-quality molecular representations. It models fixed-radius ego-nets as context and their complementary subgraphs as targets, then predicts one latent embedding from the other via a hybrid GNN-Transformer backbone—no negatives, positional encodings, or heavy preprocessing required. Pretrained on GEOM, C-FREE sets superior performance on MoleculeNet, outperforming contrastive, generative, and other multi-modal SSL methods. Fine-tuning across varied downstream datasets confirms its enhanced transferability.

strengths.value:
- Clear limitations: This paper clearly points out the main weaknesses of previous molecular graph SSL methods and gives a thorough review of contrastive and generative approaches.
- Novelty: This paper introduces a latent-predictive SSL framework for molecular graphs that provides a refreshing perspective in this field beyond traditional contrastive or generative approaches. Its core design—using ego-net to define context subgraphs and treating the remaining parts as targets, and training the model to bring their embeddings closer together—offers a distinctive method.

weaknesses.value:
- Lack of clear motivation and justification: This paper does not sufficiently explain why the embeddings of the context and target ego-nets should be close, leaving the theoretical and empirical motivation unclear. Similarly, while the target encoder is updated via EMA for stability, there is no comparison with alternative methods or evidence showing that EMA is particularly effective for the proposed architecture.
- Inconsistent and limited experimental setup: The experimental evaluation has several inconsistencies. Table 1 (linear probing) and Table 2 (full finetune) use different sets of baselines, and some baselines, especially in Table 2, exclude more recent or multimodal models, weakening the fairness of comparisons. In addition, the "4.2.2 label-efficient fine tune" and "4.2.3 modality ablation" experiments use different datasets, making it difficult to reliably verify the proposed model's effectiveness.
- Ambiguity: The model naming is somewhat confusing. Table 1 includes "C-FREE_MM_LIN" and "C-FREE_MM_DS", whereas Table 2 reports "C-FREE_MM_FULL". This inconsistency makes it unclear whether "C-FREE_MM_FULL" uses whole-molecule or subgraph-aggregated embeddings.
- Limited interpretation: This paper mainly reports numerical results without deeper discussion of why the proposed method performs well.
- Notations: References to "Table10" in Section 4.2.2 should be "Table 4", and in Table 3 the bold on "3D-FINE-TUNED" highlights a non-best result. These should be corrected.

- **RQ4 Sensitivity to k for the k-EgoNets**

This point is understandable, since k determines the EgoNet partitions and can appear central to the design. In our pre-training setup, we introduce variation by sampling ego-nets of sizes $k \in \{2, 3, 4\}$ rather than fixing a single value. Training a separate backbone for each individual k would require multiple long pre-training runs, so we opted for this mixed strategy instead.

To provide some insight into the effect of $k$ on downstream performance, we have conducted expressiveness experiments on 2D molecules with $k=1,2,3$, which give a preliminary indication of how this parameter influences the learned representations.

A more exhaustive evaluation of $k$ is currently prohibitive within the rebuttal period because each pre-training run is computationally expensive. However, we aim to include a more detailed comparison in the final version of the manuscript to better justify this choice.

---

- **RQ5 Mechanisms Preventing Latent Collapse**

The reviewer requests more insight into how the model’s latent predictions avoid collapse. This phenomenon is the subject of ongoing research, with several hypotheses proposed in the literature. One line of work suggests that updating the target encoder via an Exponential Moving Average helps stabilize training and reduce the risk of collapse [4]. Another hypothesis argues that symmetric architectures naturally converge to trivial solutions; introducing a predictor breaks this symmetry and is empirically observed to prevent collapse [5]. Even a simple two-layer MLP predictor provides noticeable improvements, while higher-capacity designs, such as transformer-based predictors, yield the strongest results.

The theoretical analysis of Wen et al [6] offers further support. In a simplified two-feature setting, they show that a trainable prediction head avoids dimensional collapse through two mechanisms: (i) the substitution effect, where strong features learned by some neurons compensate for weaker ones, and (ii) the acceleration effect, where such substitutions accelerate the learning of underdeveloped features, ultimately enabling the model to capture richer representations. Extending this intuition to higher-dimensional settings with more features and more expressive predictors, such as the transformer used here, these mechanisms are expected to be even more pronounced, thereby enhancing stability and representation quality.

---

We are grateful for the reviewer’s thoughtful feedback. We hope our responses clarify the raised points and believe that their suggestions have meaningfully strengthened our paper. We would greatly appreciate it if they could reconsider their evaluation in light of these clarifications, and we remain available to address any further questions during the rebuttal period.

---

Thank you for the clarifications and the additional experiments.
The supplementary results—such as the comparison between EgoNet and Murcko partitions, the 1-conformer setup, and the evaluation using PaiNN—helped address several of the questions I raised and made the architectural choices more understandable. The explanations regarding the predictor’s role in preventing collapse were also useful for interpreting the behavior of the framework.
Overall, these responses improved my understanding of the method, and I appreciate the authors’ efforts to provide concrete evidence and clearer justification for the design decisions.

- **RW1 & RQ1 Lack of clear motivation and justification**

We agree that the motivation for aligning context and target embeddings deserves more clarity, and we have now expanded this discussion.

In the broader self-supervised learning community, especially in vision, embedding alignment and EMA-updated target encoders remain active research topics (e.g., I-JEPA [1], BYOL [2]). Even in these influential works, the theoretical rationale is not fully settled; much of the design is guided by empirical success. We now highlight this parallel explicitly.

In Image-JEPA, the context encoder sees one part of an image while the target encoder sees a masked region from the same scene, and aligning their representations helps capture the shared underlying structure. We apply a similar idea for molecules: context and target subgraphs come from the same graph and reflect related local views of the molecule. Bringing their embeddings closer encourages the model to learn broader molecular patterns that remain stable even when looking at different fragments.

Regarding EMA, we follow the same practice as BYOL and I-JEPA, where EMA provides a smoother, more stable target encoder. While alternatives exist, there is currently no consensus on a superior choice, and EMA has become a standard, empirically robust option. We have added a more detailed discussion of how latent-predictive methods avoid representation collapse in Section 4.3, *Ablation on Predictor Types*.

---

- **RW2 & RQ2 Inconsistent and limited experimental setup**

The reviewer raises a good point regarding the differences in baseline selection between Table 1 and Table 2. We agree that this distinction is important to explain more clearly, and we will update the manuscript accordingly.

The goal of the linear-probe experiment (Table 1) is to compare our method with 2D-only baselines under exactly the same setup. These baselines are widely used and were reported with a linear-probe evaluation in [3], whose code we reuse. We include the multimodal variant of our method to show its potential benefits, while noting that this is not a fully fair comparison to 2D-only models. For this reason, we also report 2D-only results to keep the comparison balanced.

After establishing performance in the 2D linear-probe setting, the full fine-tuning experiment (Table 2) uses a different evaluation regime. Unlike the 2D baselines, which also provide linear-probe results, the multimodal models report only full fine-tuning. Re-running all of them for both pre-training and fine-tuning would require substantial computational resources, so we rely on their published setups and the reported results.

---

- **RW2 & RQ3 Ablation and Label efficient experiments use different datasets**

For Sections 4.2.2 and 4.2.3, we use the MARCEL datasets because they provide higher-quality conformer ensembles, which in turn lead to more reliable and stable downstream evaluations.

---- 

- **RW3 & RQ4 Ambiguity in Model Notation**

We thank the reviewer for pointing out the confusing notation. The suffixes *_FULL* *_LIN* *_DS* were intended to denote the evaluation setup, namely full fine-tuning vs. linear probing vs. deep-sets (which was used only in the linear probe setup and implies the use of subgraphs) but we agree that using these labels can be misleading as they don’t give the full picture on the input structure.

To remove this ambiguity, we have revised the notation to explicitly reflect the type of molecular input instead, we use :

*   *_MOL* for models operating on the full molecule, and
*   *_SUB* for models using subgraphs (which naturally corresponds to the DeepSets variant).

To directly answer the reviewer’s question: in the full fine-tuning setting, we use the full molecule.

We would like to thank Reviewer FBXr for their thoughtful review. In what follows, we clarify the Reviewer’s concerns. 

---

- **RW1: Lack of Novelty Compared to GraphJEPA**.

Reviewer FBXr notes that our method appears to be a straightforward adaptation of existing JEPA principles, as introduced in GraphJEPA. However, our approach differs in several important and substantive ways. Compared to GraphJEPA, our method removes multiple layers of architectural and algorithmic complexity, namely, we do not rely on METIS clustering, hyperbolic geometry, or positional encodings, yet we achieve stronger empirical performance. More importantly, our framework is built around the observation that 2D and 3D molecular representations provide complementary information. For example, 2D topology can capture connectivity patterns that drive reactivity and functional group interactions; in fact, most formal reaction analyses in chemistry are traditionally performed directly on 2D structures using pushing-arrow diagrams to reason about electron flow and predict plausible transformations. Meanwhile, 3D geometry is essential in scenarios where molecular conformation determines activity, such as stereoisomer-specific binding, and in capturing spatial charge distributions that underlie electrostatic properties like dipole moments and intermolecular polarization. Joining both views allows the model to reason over structural factors that each modality may not fully capture alone. Crucially, the resulting model is intentionally simple. This simplicity reduces computational and engineering overhead, making the method easier to implement, scale, and analyse, while still retaining high effectiveness.

To further support this idea, we conduct another direct comparison with GraphJEPA by reproducing their experimental setup on the ZINC dataset and using the 2D-only variant of our model. Below, we provide the results in Table 1. 

Table 1: Full fine-tuning on ZINC 

| Model         | ZINC              |
| ------------- | ----------------- |
| GraphJEPA     | 0.434 ± 0.014     |
| C-FREE (Ours) | **0.204 ± 0.015** |

Our method performs favorably compared to GraphJEPA, which suggests that some aspects of our design may better support this type of non-contrastive training. We thank the reviewer again for raising this point, since it highlights an important discussion about what JEPA-style objectives actually require in practice. We have included these results in the current revision of our paper in Table 10 and Appendix A6.

---  

* **RW2: How does 3D complement 2D?**

To address the reviewer’s question, we clarify that while we do not include an explicit structural analysis of the learned embeddings, our approach follows established observations in the molecular GNN literature [1], [2]. Permutation-equivariant 2D encoders such as GIN and GCN tend to capture topological patterns like functional groups and bond connectivity, while 3D-equivariant encoders (SchNet, PaiNN) are explicitly biased to learn geometry- and conformation-dependent signals (distances, angles, non-bonded contacts); combining the two therefore provides complementary inductive biases that improve chemical prediction. 

We also point to the linear-probe experiment with the frozen backbone as preliminary evidence that the learned representations contain transferable chemical information. Specifically, while pre-training is performed on the GEOM dataset, which primarily consists of small organic molecules with well-characterized 3D geometries, the fine-tuning tasks are drawn from MoleculeNet, encompassing a range of diverse classification datasets (e.g., BBBP, Tox21, ClinTox) that vary in molecular size, functional diversity, and property type. This distributional shift between pre-training and downstream tasks suggests that the learned embeddings capture generalizable structural features rather than overfitting to the GEOM molecules.

summary:
The paper proposes C-FREE, a non-contrastive, non-generative multimodal self-supervised molecular pretraining framework that integrates 2D topology and 3D conformations, replacing traditional contrastive/generative objectives with a JEPA-style latent predictive alignment.
I have the following questions and concerns:

1. Dependence on 3D conformations.
The best-performing variant relies on the combination of 2D molecular graphs and 3D conformers. However, obtaining high-quality 3D conformations can be computationally expensive, which may limit the practical applicability of this method to large datasets. How can this dependency on costly 3D data be mitigated? Are the 3D conformers in this work generated directly using tools such as RDKit, or do they require more precise yet expensive methods like molecular dynamics simulations or quantum chemical optimizations?
2. Chemically meaningful subgraph partitioning.
The proposed approach uses fixed-radius k-hop EgoNets to generate subgraphs, analogous to image patches, but does not incorporate chemical domain knowledge such as functional groups or bond types. Have the authors experimented with chemically informed subgraph partitions (e.g., Murcko scaffolds or functional-group-based segmentation)? If so, how do the results compare?
3. Missing stronger baselines.
The paper lacks comparisons with more recent and powerful baselines such as SCAGE, Uni-Mol and VideoMol which have demonstrated strong performance in molecular representation learning. Including such comparisons would help clarify the relative advantages of C-FREE.

strengths.value: It proposes a predictive objective based on k-EgoNet subgraphs. The model learns representations by predicting the embedding of a subgraph (target) from its complementary neighborhood (context). This integrates 2D and 3D information, and is valuable because it requires neither negative samples (avoiding the difficulties of contrastive learning) nor input graph reconstruction (avoiding the discrete reconstruction problem of generative tasks).

weaknesses.value:
1. Dependence on 3D conformations.
The best-performing variant relies on the combination of 2D molecular graphs and 3D conformers. However, obtaining high-quality 3D conformations can be computationally expensive, which may limit the practical applicability of this method to large datasets. 

2. Chemically meaningful subgraph partitioning.
The proposed approach uses fixed-radius k-hop EgoNets to generate subgraphs, analogous to image patches, but does not incorporate chemical domain knowledge such as functional groups or bond types. 

3. Missing stronger baselines.
The paper lacks comparisons with more recent and powerful baselines such as SCAGE, Uni-Mol and VideoMol which have demonstrated strong performance in molecular representation learning. Including such comparisons would help clarify the relative advantages of C-FREE.

questions.value:
1.	How can this dependency on costly 3D data be mitigated? Are the 3D conformers in this work generated directly using tools such as RDKit, or do they require more precise yet expensive methods like molecular dynamics simulations or quantum chemical optimizations?
2.	Have the authors experimented with chemically informed subgraph partitions (e.g., Murcko scaffolds or functional-group-based segmentation)? If so, how do the results compare?
3.	Could some comparative experiments be added?

-  **RW1 & RQ1 Dependence on 3D conformations**

We thank reviewers FBXr and 8F9v for noting that more detail on the computational costs of using 3D conformers would strengthen the paper. Below, we expand on our design choices and clarify how we handle these costs.

Regarding the generation of these conformers, we rely on the GEOM dataset, which provides pre-computed 3D structures. These are not generated on the fly using RDKit alone. In GEOM, initial molecular geometries are first generated with RDKit, then optimized using GFN2-xTB [1], and finally sampled with CREST [2]. This multi-step procedure ensures accurate and diverse 3D structures, which are more reliable than simple RDKit embeddings.

Nevertheless, the conformers used for MoleculeNet fine-tuning are generated with RDKit. However, our method also remains competitive in the purely 2D setting, when no conformers and 3D GNNs are used (see MoleculeNet linear-probe results in Table 1). Additionally, by precomputing multiple context-target pairs for each subgraph, we also eliminate on-the-fly processing, further reducing computational overhead.

While the 3D conformer ensemble is a central component of our approach, our framework can effectively avoid the associated computational cost and still achieve strong performance in 2D-only scenarios.

---

- **RW2 & RQ2 Chemically meaningful subgraph partitioning**

The reviewer’s comment on our design choices is important, and we are happy to clarify our reasoning. Our aim is to keep the model simple while remaining flexible. By using ego-nets, we avoid domain-specific engineering while keeping the framework broadly applicable. Analogous to patch-based approaches in computer vision, where patches contain only part of the input yet still support learning meaningful structure, ego-nets present the model with molecular subgraphs from which it can learn the underlying chemical relationships during training.

To evaluate this suggestion directly, we run an additional experiment comparing our pre-trained backbone with a variant trained using Murcko-based fragments. In this variant, the Murcko scaffold of each molecule is used as the target subgraph and the remainder as the context, which lets us assess the effect of using chemically informed fragments. Both methods are evaluated on the MoleculeNet datasets (Table 1a) and follow the same evaluation protocol.

Table 1a: Evaluation of C-FREE pre-trained using EgoNets vs. Murcko scaffolds on MoleculeNet
| Method          | BBBP     | Tox21    | ToxCast  | SIDER    | Clintox  | MUV      | HIV      | BACE     | Average  |
| --------------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- | -------- |
| C-FREE (EgoNet) | 78.9     | 84.2     | **71.7** | 62.5     | **83.7** | **82.5** | 77.9     | 78.6     | **77.5** |
| C-FREE (Murcko) | **87.6** | **85.9** | 67.8     | **63.7** | 83.4     | 70.9     | **81.0** | **80.5** | **77.6** |

For ClinTox, MUV, and ToxCast, we observe a slight decrease in performance. In addition, we repeat this experiment on the QM9 dataset (Table 1b). Here, we observe gains on the R2 and ZPVE targets, whereas the Ego-Net variant performs best on the remaining four tasks.

Overall, these results suggest that our EgoNet-based approach already learns useful structural patterns without relying on hand-crafted chemical knowledge, while still performing competitively across diverse tasks.

* **RQ1 Computational cost.** 

The concern about the computational cost of added conformations raised by reviewers FBXr and 8F9v is valid. We note, however, that our method performs strongly in the purely 2D setting (see the MoleculeNet linear-probe results in Table 1) without relying on conformers or the more expensive 3D GNN. In addition, by precomputing multiple context–target pairs for each subgraph, we avoid on-the-fly generation and keep the computational overhead low.

Below, we present a runtime comparison of the pre-training and fine-tuning costs of C-FREE and GraphMVP. Most of the training overhead is from the double forward passes through the target and context encoders. However, during fine-tuning, C-FREE achieves a runtime comparable to GraphMVP. Due to the time constraints of the rebuttal phase, we were unable to conduct additional runtime experiments; however, we will include comparisons with MoleBlend and 3D InfoMax in the final version of the paper.

Runtimes are averaged over 6 epochs (Pre-train: 50K GEOM,  Fine-Tuning: 8K Tox21 - batch size = 32).

summary.value:
This paper introduces a contrast-free predictive framework for molecular self-supervised pretraining that jointly learns from 2D molecular graphs and 3D conformer ensembles.
The main idea is to:

- Divide each molecule into multiple k-EgoNet subgraphs,
- Construct context–target pairs for latent-space prediction, and
- Integrate 3D conformer information through a hybrid GINE + SchNet + Transformer backbone.

The proposed method reports state-of-the-art results on benchmarks including MoleculeNet, Kraken, and Drugs-75K.

strengths.value:
1. Clear motivation and simplicity

The paper clearly identifies the weaknesses of existing contrastive or generative molecular SSL approaches—namely, difficulties in defining negatives, instability in discrete reconstruction, and inconsistency in augmentation design. The proposed contrast-free predictive formulation provides a simple and effective alternative that avoids these issues.

2. Theoretical grounding

The use of DeepSets-based subgraph aggregation provides an expressive model comparable to ESAN.
The paper includes a theoretical argument showing that the proposed framework is more expressive than 1-WL.

3. Comprehensive experimentation

The experiments span a wide range of evaluations, including frozen backbone probing, full fine-tuning, label-efficiency analysis, ablations, and expressiveness studies. The design maintains strong consistency between pretraining and fine-tuning (EgoNet pretraining combined with DeepSets fine-tuning). The ablation on the predictor component effectively demonstrates its role in avoiding representation collapse.

weaknesses.value:
1. Limited technical depth

The C-FREE framework closely follows existing contrast-free latent prediction paradigms such as BYOL, I-JEPA, and BGRL. Its novelty mainly lies in the use of EgoNet-based subgraph sampling and the integration of 2D and 3D modalities.
While applying such modern self-supervised techniques to the molecular domain is reasonable and well executed, the paper lacks deeper analysis of what kind of chemical or structural knowledge the model actually captures — for example, whether the learned representations encode functional groups, chirality, or spatial interaction patterns.
Including such analysis would have strengthened the scientific novelty of the work, showing that the model learns chemically meaningful concepts rather than only demonstrating performance gains.
Overall, the contribution feels more like a well-engineered domain adaptation than a fundamentally new conceptual advance.

2. Baseline comparability

It is not entirely clear whether all baseline models were trained with the same data, number of conformers, or backbone settings, which makes the performance comparisons less transparent.

3. Choice of encoders not well justified

The method relies on GINE for 2D graphs and SchNet for 3D conformers, even though newer and more expressive GNN architectures—such as GNS, EGNN, SphereNet, GemNet, or SE(3)-Transformer—are now available.
The authors do not explain why these relatively older encoders were chosen or whether using stronger graph networks might yield further gains.

questions.value:
1. Could the authors elaborate on what specific chemical or structural knowledge the learned embeddings capture (e.g., functional groups, chirality, or geometric motifs)?

2. Were all baseline models trained on identical data and conformer setups? If not, how might differences affect the reported comparisons?

3. Why were GINE and SchNet chosen as encoders instead of more modern architectures (e.g., EGNN, SphereNet, GemNet, or SE(3)-Transformer)?

4. How sensitive is the model’s performance to the choice of k in the EgoNet subgraph partitioning?

5. Could the authors provide more insight into how the model’s latent predictions avoid collapse beyond the predictor ablation results?

* **RW3 & RQ2 MoleculeNet Limitations and Evaluation on 3D-heavy datasets.** 

The reviewer raises a valid point about the known limitations of MoleculeNet. We include it in our experiments because it remains a standard benchmark in the literature, which helps keep our results comparable to prior work. To provide a more complete evaluation, we also report results on QM9 and SPICE (see Tables 2–3) as well as ZINC (see Table 1), which offer a broader set of molecules and properties.

For all experiments, we use the same pre-trained backbone as in our main results and fully fine-tune the models. For QM9 and SPICE, we restrict the model to its 3D encoder, ensuring our results are directly comparable to those of the 3D backbones UniMol, GEM, and TensorNet.

On the ZINC benchmark (Table 1), our method shows a clear performance improvement over GraphJEPA. This suggests that the gains come not just from the use of EgoNets, but from the combination of architectural choices and the overall training pipeline, with EgoNets contributing as one part of this broader design.

On QM9 (Table 2), we compare our model against UniMol2 and GEM. Our model achieves better performance on four of the six evaluated targets, despite using significantly fewer parameters than UniMol2 (our pre-trained encoder has 8M parameters, while UniMol2 uses 1.1B). The only exceptions are the HOMO/LUMO/Gap and ZPVE predictions, where UniMol2 retains a slight advantage.

On SPICE (Table 3), our method achieves results competitive with TensorNet and outperforms the Equivariant Transformer.
